title: Does this lighting system work for a stylized isometric game?
author: Kiko_Production
selftext:
Quick shader test for my city builder.  
I’m trying to keep the assets looking hand-painted while still having dynamic time of day, directional shadows, normal maps and emissive lighting.  
AI helped generate some of the normal maps and a few supporting assets, while the lighting/shader setup itself is being built in Godot.  
Still rough, but I’m curious:  
Does the day/night transition look convincing?  
And is there anything about the shadows or normal-map lighting that immediately feels wrong?

replies.author: Smok3dSalmon
replies.body:
Too many straight lines and the black outlines on the buildings. To me it’s a giveaway that it’s computer graphics and not painted. The dark patches on the grass kinda give me a feeling that it’s painted, but the hard edges on the paths also feel very much like computer graphics.

I also think isometric is not really a perspective that’s common in painting and it feels very mathematical and architecturally precise. 

The grass, trees, foliage, and house texture looks closer to painting and I like the window illumination. 

Look at Thomas Kinkade’s Evening in the Forest, you can see the brush strokes and the texture or the canvas and paint. 

There is also s great video on YouTube about the art style of 
11-11: Memories Retold which is a game that has a unique art style.

If you want to keep outlines, you could look at Studio Ghibli, I believe the outlines in those anime movies are inconsistent and feel a lot more hand drawn.

I think the artwork is still, ok so I’m not trying to just shit on it. Hopefully this is constructive.

With the rise of cell-shaded art of XIII or Borderlands, your game feels more like that instead of an actual painting.

One quick thing, I had Astra do the same exact things with those shadows btw - transparent polygons (at least not rendered) but they still allow the ground be occluded or shadowed or whatever behind them. However, after looking at those “lollipops” I had Astra analyze each tree, count the major “lobes” of foliage, and then place that many spheres in kind of a blob type thing - then I asked it to break up the spheres by adding polygonal shapes/texture onto the spheres. 

Do it. It makes a world of difference.

replies.author: Kiko_Production
replies.body:
Yeah, that’s actually why I’m trying not to make it just another city builder.  
Before this I was working on a roguelike with some unusual mechanics, but I eventually had to put it on hold. I wanted a distinctive art style that didn’t immediately look AI-generated, and the sheer amount of animation needed, while keeping all the characters and enemies visually consistent became a huge bottleneck for me as a solo dev.  
So I decided to shelve it until I either find an artist to work with or get good enough to handle that pipeline myself.  
City Paradise is kind of my learning/capstone project to get deeper into gamedev and build a much better pipeline for future games.  
The main hook I’m experimenting with here is mixing a **city builder with a dating sim**.  
I’m not really aiming for a super deep SimCity-style simulation though. I want it to be much more casual something where you can just sit down, build a nice little city, watch it grow, and at the same time talk to the characters responsible for different parts of it.  
So instead of separating the city management and character side, I want them to affect each other. Building your relationship with someone could unlock new options, bonuses, buildings or changes for the part of the city they manage.  
Basically something cozy and easy to get into, but with enough character interaction and progression to give it its own identity.
